presentingComplaint: Found drowsy at home surrounded by empty medication blister packs, brought in by ambulance after a brief witnessed convulsion.
history: 27-year-old woman with a background of recurrent depressive disorder, brought to the emergency department by ambulance after her partner found her unresponsive on the sofa with several empty amitriptyline blister packs and a partially written note. Best estimate is ingestion of roughly 50 tablets of amitriptyline 25 mg (~1.25 g) around 2 hours before arrival, with an unquantified amount of vodka. En route, paramedics documented a GCS of 10, a brief self-terminating generalised tonic-clonic seizure, and a broad-complex tachycardia with a systolic of 82 mmHg. Because of the wide-complex tachycardia and hypotension the receiving team initially activated a parallel cardiac pathway, and the seizure with reduced consciousness prompted a concurrent stroke/CT-head referral; collateral history of the empty tricyclic packs and the anticholinergic toxidrome clarified the true diagnosis. No prior cardiac disease, no chest pain reported before collapse. Regular medication is amitriptyline only; no anticoagulants, no recreational drug use reported.
examination: Drowsy but rousable to voice (GCS E3V4M6 = 13 after the seizure), warm dry flushed skin, dry mucous membranes, dilated poorly reactive pupils (~6 mm), no focal neurological deficit and normal tone/reflexes symmetrically. Bladder palpable (urinary retention). Chest clear, no added heart sounds or murmur, calves soft. No neck stiffness, no rash. Bowel sounds sluggish. Cardiac monitor shows sinus tachycardia with broad QRS complexes.

labs.ecg: Sinus tachycardia rate 128; QRS 132 ms; prominent terminal R wave in aVR (>3 mm) with rightward terminal 40 ms axis; no ST-elevation, no reciprocal changes

imaging: Non-contrast CT head: no intracranial haemorrhage, no infarct, no mass. CXR: clear lung fields, normal cardiac silhouette. Bedside echo: hyperdynamic non-dilated LV, no regional wall-motion abnormality, no effusion.
microbiology: Not applicable - non-infective toxicological presentation; no fever source, blood cultures not indicated.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute coronary syndrome / cardiogenic shock (raised by broad-complex tachycardia + hypotension)
finalDiagnosis: Acute amitriptyline (tricyclic antidepressant) poisoning with sodium-channel-blockade cardiotoxicity, anticholinergic toxidrome, seizure and hypotension - the broad-complex tachycardia and seizure mimicked cardiac and neurological emergencies but reflect drug toxicity.
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Poisoning and Drug Overdose
American Heart Association - Management of Patients with Cardiac Arrest or Life-Threatening Toxicity due to Poisoning 2023
AACT/EAPCCT - Position Statement: Gastrointestinal Decontamination / Single-Dose Activated Charcoal 2013
stewardship: No antimicrobial therapy indicated. This is a non-infective toxicological emergency; fever is low-grade and attributable to the anticholinergic toxidrome/seizure rather than infection. Antibiotics should be withheld unless an objective source of infection emerges. Management is supportive and antidotal (serum/urinary alkalinisation).
contraindications: Flumazenil is contraindicated - can precipitate seizures and unmask arrhythmia in mixed/TCA overdose.
Class Ia, Ic and III antiarrhythmics contraindicated - worsen sodium-channel blockade.
Physostigmine contraindicated in TCA toxicity - risk of asystole and seizures.
Avoid activated charcoal if airway unprotected and consciousness reduced (aspiration risk) - secure airway first.
edgeCases: QRS >100 ms predicts seizures and >160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia - the ECG, not drug levels, guides treatment.
Serum TCA levels do not correlate with severity and should not delay bicarbonate therapy.
Always screen for co-ingested paracetamol and salicylate even when the drug appears identified.
Terminal R wave in aVR helps distinguish TCA cardiotoxicity from primary ischaemic broad-complex tachycardia.
Alkalinisation target arterial pH 7.50-7.55; hypokalaemia from bicarbonate must be monitored.
expectedMaiK: Recognise the sodium-channel-blocker (tricyclic) toxidrome - broad QRS, anticholinergic signs, seizure, hypotension - and treat with IV sodium bicarbonate boluses for QRS widening/arrhythmia/hypotension while securing the airway; this is a toxicological emergency, not a primary cardiac or cerebrovascular event.
expectedNextQuestions: What exactly was taken, how many tablets, and at what time?
Were any other drugs, paracetamol-containing products, or alcohol co-ingested?
Is there a suicide note or stated intent, and what is the psychiatric history?
What was the pre-hospital GCS trend and were there further seizures?
Any known cardiac disease or QT-prolonging medication?
expectedInvestigations: Serial 12-lead ECG (QRS duration, terminal R in aVR)
Electrolytes, renal function, glucose and creatine kinase
CT head if no rapid improvement or focal signs
regressionAssertions: Engine diagnosis resolves to drug_intox (tricyclic/sodium-channel-blocker poisoning).
Broad QRS + terminal R in aVR + anticholinergic toxidrome must not be misclassified as acs.
IV sodium bicarbonate is first-line for QRS widening and hypotension.
Flumazenil and class Ia/Ic/III antiarrhythmics flagged as contraindicated.
